newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - Dutch HBG 1996 net up 7 percent.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dutch HBG 1996 net up 7 percent.

text.p: Dutch builder Hollandsche Beton Groep reported 1996 net profits up seven percent at 111 million guilders ($58.5 million) on Tuesday and said it expected to hold profits steady over the current financial year.
The Netherlands' largest builder also announced it planned a 10-for-one share split and said it would lift its 1996 dividend to 13.40 guilders per share from a year-earlier 12.80.

"We are pleased to report the forecast slight rise in earnings...which we achieved without the considerable extraordinary gains of previous years," HBG chairman Nic de Ronde Bresser told a results news conference.
HBG reported an extraordinary loss of 10 million guilders over 1996, compared with a gain of seven million in 1995.
The earnings came in at the top of the forecast range, as analysts had forecast 1996 net profit before extraordinaries of 106-120 million guilders, with consensus at 115 million.
De Ronde Bresser said HBG had been able to benefit from a buoyant Dutch construction market, which accounted for 41 percent of group turnover last year.
Britain, which accounted for some 21 percent of turnover, had remained difficult and could well take two years to recover, he said. Nevertheless HBG's British operations had all remained in profit.
The construction activities of London Stock Exchange-listed Higgs&Hill, acquired last December, posted a loss of 5.8 million pounds sterling, De Ronde Bresser said.
The unit, to be incorporated alongside HBG's other activities in a new company, was included in HBG's 1996 balance sheet, but not in the profit and loss account, he said.
HBG sees the Higgs&Hill loss evening out in 1997.
"The acquisition in England will have no positive or negative contribution to make," finance director Dick Sinninghe Damste said.

In Germany the market outlook remained poor and German unit Raulf Bau closed 1996 with an unspecified loss. However losses had been capped and the company was seen breaking even in 1997, Sinninghe Damste said.

Germany accounted for 11 percent of group turnover in 1996, but in 1997 this share is seen mushrooming to 35 percent as a result of the acquisition last December of a 74 percent stake in Wayss&Freytag.
The German bourse-listed company, which earlier posted a 1996 loss of 90 million marks, was expected to perform significantly better in 1997, Sinninghe Damste said.
"Wayss&Freitag will show a significant improvement and will have a neutral effect on HBG's result (in 1997)," he said.
The two acquisitions will take group turnover to an estimated 10 billion guilders in 1997, from 5.8 billion in 1996.
Outside Europe, where HBG's activities were more project-oriented, the builder had been able to opt for higher margin markets, De Ronde Bresser said.
"On balance activities outside Europe achieved a positive result," he said.
Dredging also contributed substantially to results and corporate strategy was aimed at bolstering HBG's position as one of the leading players in this market, he added.
De Ronde Bresser said HBG had decided to split its shares in response to repeated urging from its shareholders.
On the Amsterdam Stock Exchange investors welcomed the news, sending HBG shares 12.00 guilders higher to 422.00 at 1400 GMT.
